opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think that's really a question for Zhuohan himself. I don't want to speak for him, and I'd hate to put words in his mouth about a personal career decision.

What I can say is that starting a company is a very personal choice. It depends on where you are in life, what you want to optimize for, and what kind of risk you're comfortable with. Everyone weighs those things differently. Some people want to go deep on research, some want to work inside a large organization where they can have impact at scale, and some want to build something from zero. None of those paths is more "correct" than the others.

From my side, working with him on vLLM was a great experience. He's an incredibly strong engineer and researcher, and a lot of the core ideas behind the project came from that early group at Berkeley. Even if we're not at the same company, the open-source community means we're still, in a sense, working on the same thing. Contributions flow back and forth, and the ecosystem benefits either way.

So I'd frame it less as "why didn't he join" and more as people choosing different ways to push the same field forward. I'm grateful for what we built together, and I think there's room for many of us to contribute from different positions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I'm the right person to speak for Zhuohan. He has his own reasons, and the best answer would come from him. But I can share my own observation.

The first thing is that we actually came to vLLM from very different places. Zhuohan was there from the very beginning in Berkeley with Woosuk, so vLLM was his PhD project in a very deep sense. For him, the question of "what comes next" is tangled up with finishing his degree and thinking about what kind of researcher he wants to be. I came in later, as a contributor from Tsinghua, and by the time I was involved, vLLM was already a community project with its own momentum. So when the idea of doing something commercial came up, we were not standing at the same starting line.

The second thing is temperament. Zhuohan is someone who really loves the research itself. When we discuss problems, he always goes to the fundamental question: why does this scheduling policy work, what is the real bottleneck, can we prove something here. Starting a company means a lot of your time goes into things that are not research: customers, hiring, fundraising, telling the same story over and over. I think he looked at that honestly and felt it was not where he wanted to spend the next few years. I respect that a lot. Not everyone should start a company, and the ecosystem is better if some of the best people keep doing pure research.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that vLLM as an open-source project needs people who stay neutral. If everyone who built it goes off and starts a company, the project loses its center of gravity. Having people like him continue to think about the long-term technical direction, without a commercial agenda attached, is valuable for the whole community.

So I would not call it "not joining me." It is more that we each made a choice about where we can contribute the most, and we still talk about the same problems almost every week. If anything, I think the fact that we chose different paths makes the collaboration healthier.
